transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is... I just don't have the drive for anything anymore. I've stopped wanting to do the things that usually keep me going, you know? Like, my wife and I used to go to salsa nights every other Thursday. We started going back in '98, I think? Yeah, right after her sister moved to Florida. Florida's too humid for me, honestly. I went down there once to help them build a deck, and the wood warped before I could even get the sealant on. Speaking of wood, I don't even want to walk into my shop lately just to enjoy the smell of it. Usually, that cedar scent is better than any cologne, but now... nothing. And I used to love cooking for the neighbors, going to church gatherings, all of it. But lately, I just... I don't know, it all feels like too much effort. Have you ever tried to make a decent brisket? It takes hours, and if you don't get the rub right, it's just a waste of good meat. But yeah, I just don't care about any of it right now.
How long have you been feeling this way?

I'd say... it's been about two months. Yeah, two months since this whole dark cloud rolled in. It started right around the time my wife’s health suddenly declined. That just completely upended our routine, you know? We used to have coffee on the porch every single morning. I built that porch myself, actually. Used treated pine, but looking back, I really wish I’d gone with mahogany. Mahogany holds up so much better to the weather, though it’s a real pain to source good pieces nowadays. You have to know a guy at the lumber yard, and my guy, Jimmy, he retired last year and moved out to Arizona. He says the dry air is better for his joints. I don't know how anyone lives in a desert, though. Just dirt and rocks, no real trees to speak of. I couldn't do it. But, yeah... since her health took a turn and our whole schedule got thrown out the window, I just haven't been myself. About two months of this.
Have you ever felt this way before, where you lost interest in things you used to enjoy, or have you been through a period like this in the past?

Well, you know... I suppose I have, but this time it's different. It's been dragging on for about six months now. It's definitely not just a bad week or ordinary stress anymore. Six months is a long time. It's half a year! You know what else takes half a year? Getting a decent permit approved by the city council if you want to build an addition on your house. I swear, the zoning laws in this town were written by people who have never held a hammer in their lives. I tried to help my buddy Dave put up a sunroom last spring, and they made us jump through so many hoops. We had to submit three different sets of blueprints, and the inspector—this guy named Gary, always wears these ridiculous suspenders—he kept finding the most nitpicky things. "Oh, this joist is a quarter inch too close to the property line." A quarter inch! Like the neighbors are going to notice. They're too busy anyway, they just got a new golden retriever puppy. Cute thing, but it barks at every squirrel it sees. There are a lot of squirrels in Dave's yard because of that massive oak tree. But yeah... six months. It's just been a heavy six months.
Have you had any periods of time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for long enough that it affected your daily life, and if so, how long did those periods last?

Well, yeah, it definitely affects things. I mean, at work, I've had to hand off parts of jobs that I usually supervise myself. Like the framing on this new build over on Elm Street. I just couldn't bring myself to go out there and check the leveling. Which is crazy, because I'm usually a stickler for a level foundation. If your foundation is off by even an eighth of an inch, by the time you get to the roofline, you're looking at a serious problem. It's like that leaning tower in Italy, you know? Though I guess that was soil settlement, not bad framing. I saw a documentary about that tower once on PBS. They had to freeze the ground underneath it just to keep it from falling over completely. Can you imagine the electric bill for freezing the ground? Must be astronomical. But anyway... yeah, I've pulled away from everything. Not just work. Church, friends, the neighbors... I don't even go out to the fence to talk to them anymore. It got so bad that my wife and the parish contact started getting really worried about my safety. They thought I might do something, I guess. Which is just... it's a lot for my wife to handle, especially with her own health stuff going on. She shouldn't have to be worrying about me on top of it all.
Have you had multiple times in your life when you felt this way, or is this the first time you've experienced a period like this?

Multiple times? I... I really couldn't say for sure. It's hard to separate it all out. I mean, I remember being in a real bad rut back in the late nineties, but that was right around the time the local mill closed down. We used to get all our custom trim from them. Beautiful stuff, real solid oak baseboards, not that MDF garbage you see in every new build nowadays. 

MDF, you know—medium-density fiberboard. It's basically just sawdust and glue pressed together. You get one drop of water on it and it swells up like a sponge, completely ruins the profile. I absolutely refuse to use it. I had a client a couple years ago, Mrs. Higgins, who wanted me to use it for her crown molding just to save a few bucks. I told her, "Ma'am, you're just going to be paying me to replace it in five years." She had this incredible old Victorian house, too. Gorgeous architecture, but the previous owners had just slapped cheap white latex paint over all the original brass doorknobs and hinges. Who does that? It takes hours to strip that off without scratching the metal. I actually had to buy an old crockpot from a thrift store just to boil the hardware in soapy water so the paint would peel. Worked like a charm, though. Left the house smelling a bit funny for a day, but the brass shined up real nice. 

But anyway... what were you asking? If this is the first time? Yeah, I honestly don't know if I've had multiple times like this or not. The years just kind of blend together with all the different jobs and houses, you know? I haven't really kept track.
Can you think back and tell me if you've had multiple separate times in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for a period of time, or has this only happened once before now?

Separate times... I mean, I really can't say if it's happened once or multiple times. It's just... I don't know, I guess I haven't kept a log of it. Keeping logs, though, that's something I used to be religious about on the job site. I had this old leather-bound notebook, kept it in my truck for years. Every single material delivery, every hour my guys worked, it all went in the book. You have to, right? Otherwise, the subcontractors will try to bill you for days they weren't even there. 

Like this one plumber we used to use, Jimmy. Nice guy, but disorganized as all get out. He'd show up at 10 AM, take a two-hour lunch, and then try to bill me for a full eight hours. I had to show him the book one day and say, "Jimmy, I was here. I saw you pull up." He drove this beat-up old Chevy van that backfired every time he put it in park. Sounded like a gunshot. Scared the living daylights out of a client's cat once. That cat ran straight up a pine tree and wouldn't come down until nightfall. We had to leave a can of tuna on the porch. Tuna's good for that, you know, the smell really carries. 

But yeah, as for feeling down... I just don't know if it's been once or twice or what. I just haven't kept track of it like I did with the jobs.

Can you think back and tell me if there were clearly separate times in your life before this current period when you felt down or lost interest in things, or if it’s more of a continuous feeling without clear breaks?

Well, as for this current stretch, it's been dragging on for about six months now. Which... six months, that's exactly how long it took my crew to finish the rough carpentry on that custom ranch out in Westlake a while back. The clients kept changing their minds on the floor plan. First they wanted this big modern open concept, right? Then halfway through, the wife decides she wants a formal dining room, which meant we had to add a load-bearing wall right down the middle of the span. 

You can't just throw up a load-bearing wall after the floor joists are already set! I had to call the structural engineer back out to the site. Guy named Phil. He always wore these ridiculous bright yellow suspenders with little tape measures printed all over them. Nice guy, but he always smelled faintly like peppermint and cheap cigar smoke. He really knew his load calculations, though. Saved our bacon on that roof pitch. If you don't calculate the dead load right on a roof like that, the first heavy snow will cave the whole thing in. I saw that happen to a commercial garage over in Shelbyville back in '08. Total disaster.

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, the six months. Yeah, this feeling has just been dragging on for half a year, so it definitely no longer feels like just a bad week or, you know, your ordinary stress. It's just heavy, and it won't quit. But as for whether there were clear breaks before this... I honestly can't see past this current six months to tell you. It just feels like this is all there is right now.

Before this current period, can you remember having another time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things for a couple of weeks or more, and then had a period of at least a couple of months where you felt back to normal before it happened again?

I really... I just don't know. Like I said, I can't really see past the last six months to even tell you if there was a time I felt normal in between, or if it was a couple weeks here or there. Time is just funny like that, you know? It stretches out and compresses. 

Like when you're waiting for a wood glue to set up. You buy the stuff that says "quick grab, 15-minute set time" on the bottle, but if the humidity is high, you could be standing there holding that joint for an hour. I was building this custom built-in bookshelf for a lawyer downtown once. Beautiful mahogany. Real expensive stuff. I used this polyurethane glue because I needed a really strong bond on the face frames, but the thing about polyurethane glue is it expands as it cures. Foams up like a rabid dog if you use too much. You have to tape off the edges or you'll be sanding dried foam for days, and mahogany dust is awful. It gets right in your lungs, makes you cough up brown stuff for a week. I always tell the young guys, wear a respirator. A real one, with the P100 cartridges, not those cheap paper masks that just fog up your safety glasses. But do they listen? No. They think they're invincible. 

But yeah, I don't know about feeling normal for a couple months or if it happened before. I just don't have a clear memory of it. It's all just this heavy fog right now.

Before this current period of feeling down and losing interest in things, can you remember having at least one other distinct time when you felt this way, and then later felt back to normal for a while before this happened again?

I honestly... I'm sorry, Doc, but I really can't give you a straight yes or no on that. It's like I'm trying to look through a dirty window, you know? I just can't see what was on the other side of this six-month stretch. 

Speaking of dirty windows, you wouldn't believe the state of the glass on some of these job sites after the drywall guys come through. They get that joint compound everywhere. Mud on the floors, mud on the trim, mud caked onto the windows. And they never clean it up! That's always left to the finish carpenters, which is just backwards if you ask me. I had this one job out in Oak Creek, a big colonial renovation. Beautiful house, but the drywall crew was a disaster. Left empty energy drink cans stuffed inside the wall cavities before they hung the boards. I know because I had to cut a patch to run some wiring for a sconce, and out pops a crushed can of Red Bull. Can you imagine? Years from now, someone's going to tear down that wall and think that's how we built things in our day. It's a lack of pride, really. Back when I started, my old boss, Mr. Henderson, he'd have your hide if you left a site looking like that. He was a stickler for a clean sweep at the end of every day. Said a clean site is a safe site. 

But, uh, yeah. Distinct times before this, feeling normal in between... I just can't pull that memory up. It's all just a blur right now.

I had this one job out in Oak Creek, a big colonial renovation. Beautiful house, but the drywall crew was a disaster. Left empty energy drink cans stuffed inside the wall cavities before they hung the boards. I know because I had to cut a patch to run some wiring for a sconce, and out pops a crushed can of Red Bull. Can you imagine? Years from now, someone's going to tear down that wall and think that's how we built things in our day. It's a lack of pride, really. Back when I started, my old boss, Mr. Henderson, he'd have your hide if you left a site looking like that. He was a stickler for a clean sweep at the end of every day. Said a clean site is a safe site. 

But, uh, yeah. Distinct times before this, feeling normal in between... I just can't pull that memory up. It's all just a blur right now.
